description: Generated existing-evidence snapshot; not a Haiti assessment or infrastructure-protection estimate.

records.mitigation_mechanism: The silvopasture study in this cell compared silvopasture with non-grazed managed forest in Washington State, USA: silvopasture management reduced grass biomass, litter and duff depth, and the authors conclude that managing overstory, understory and grazing together can reduce fuel loads and potential wildfire risk [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_t3_litter_duff_batcheler24_5]. Rotational grazing removes understory biomass and herbaceous surface fuel, and the reduced, more variable overstory density has the potential to reduce fire frequency compared with other land uses [ev_t3_herbaceous_fuel_batcheler24_4, ev_t3_fire_freq_batcheler24_3]. Rate of fire spread and burn severity correlate with litter and duff depth in this forest type, which is why the litter reduction matters for fire [ev_t3_fire_spread_batcheler24_6]. A land-use overlay of burnt areas across six European Mediterranean countries found that, corrected for the extent of each land use, agroforestry occupied 12% of the area but was associated with only 6% of the fires, while shrubland occupied 16% and was associated with 40%; agroforestry's share was not statistically different from that of forest and grassland [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_1, ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_2]. Before that correction, the average share of fire incidents was lowest for grasslands (11.2%) and agroforestry (20.2%) and highest for shrublands (36.7%) and forests (31.9%) [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_3]. Separately, a Kenyan compiler for farmer managed natural regeneration rates that tree cover can increase the risk of major wild fires, and that fire breaks should be considered for larger sites [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk].
records.caveats: None of this evidence can set the class. Every comparison is against the unmanaged state rather than the farming-system counterfactual this cell asks about. The US study compares silvopasture with non-grazed managed forest [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_t3_litter_duff_batcheler24_5, ev_t3_select_fuels_batcheler24_8], and the Mediterranean overlay compares existing grazed wood-pasture with forest, shrubland and grassland, not with the cropland or open pasture a project would convert [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_1, ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_3]. Against treeless pasture the reading changes: introducing trees adds woody material, litter and duff that open pasture does not have, so having less fuel than a forest does not mean having less fuel than the pasture the practice replaces. Read against that comparator, the fire-spread correlation with litter and duff depth would point to added risk rather than a reduction [ev_t3_fire_spread_batcheler24_6], and in the Mediterranean data grassland, not agroforestry, had the lowest unadjusted share of fires [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_3]. The Mediterranean result that does favour agroforestry is the one against shrubland; against forest and grassland the difference was not significant [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_2]. Both studies come from high-income settings outside the LIC/LMIC target; in the US study only select fuel types fell (1-, 10-, 100- and 1000-h fuels were similar between the management systems), and the fire-frequency statement is a potential effect, not a measurement [ev_t3_select_fuels_batcheler24_8, ev_t3_fire_freq_batcheler24_3]. What would fill the gap is a fire-risk comparison (fuel load, fire frequency or burn severity) of agroforestry against the treeless farmland or pasture it replaces, ideally in an LIC/LMIC system. The Kenyan WOCAT rating is carried but cannot set the class either: it is a practitioner judgement, not a measurement [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk]. It concerns natural regeneration rather than silvopasture, but its direction agrees with the comparator argument above: added tree cover adds fuel, and the compiler recommends fire breaks for larger sites [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk]. The study systems are agro-pastoral (silvopasture and grazed wood-pasture), and the cell is applied to all farming systems by default [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_1].

records.mitigation_mechanism: In Vietnam, a review citing Nguyen et al. 2013 reports that farms with trees were less affected by an extreme flood that caused heavy crop losses in the region [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_11]. In Isiolo County, Kenya, households said trees planted in a line stop soil being swept away by water, and the study concludes that agroforestry builds livelihood resilience to floods [ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6, ev_t3_flood_conclusion_quandt17_11]. In Nyando District, Kenya, farmers reported that tree roots prevented extensive soil erosion and soil fertility loss during the floods, and some had fruit from their trees as their only steady food when other crops were underwater or washed away [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_1]. The same review also reports, citing Eychène et al. 2014, that in Mesoamerica coffee-based agroforestry can help prevent flood occurrences, reducing the adverse impact of extreme rainfall events [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12].
records.caveats: The Vietnamese result is cited second-hand and the 40% figure in it is the regional crop loss, not the effect of trees [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_11]. The Kenyan household units come from a single study of farmer interviews in a semi-arid area, and the line-planting unit concerns soil erosion by water as a component of flood impact [ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6]. The Nyando flood units are farmer-reported, from interviews and focus groups, and enter through soil erosion and food supply as components of flood impact [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_1]. The Mesoamerican coffee statement is a crop-specific, second-hand review citation with no country, income group or size recorded [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12]. Every unit reports a benefit, but none says how large it is, so the class is a slight reduction; all the field evidence is from lower-middle-income Kenya and Vietnam [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_11, ev_t3_flood_conclusion_quandt17_11].

records.mitigation_mechanism: Household case studies in two communities of Isiolo County, Kenya, conclude that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to floods and drought [ev_t3_flood_conclusion_quandt17_11]. The quote does not describe a physical process by which trees reduce flood impact, nor how large the reduction is [ev_t3_flood_conclusion_quandt17_11].
records.caveats: The row rests on a single Kenyan study (lower-middle income, semi-arid, mixed crop–livestock) inside the LIC/LMIC target, and on the study's overall conclusion from what interviewees reported [ev_t3_flood_conclusion_quandt17_11]. The quote speaks of agroforestry in general rather than a planted silvoarable design, and it does not say how severe the floods were, so nothing here speaks to severe or extreme floods [ev_t3_flood_conclusion_quandt17_11]. The source system is mixed crop–livestock, applied to all farming systems by default. A second independent source, ideally with a measured flood loss with and without trees, is what this cell needs.

records.effect_mechanism: A sub-Saharan meta-analysis found agroforestry five and ten times better than controls for runoff and soil loss respectively [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1]. A pantropical meta-analysis found agroforestry trees reduced soil erosion by 50% against crop monocultures, and stated mechanisms include greater soil cover and structure protecting against raindrop impact, roots aiding infiltration and reducing surface runoff, and live fences lowering runoff velocity; runoff reduction is used as a component [ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_santos25_2, ev_runoff_reduction_watts22_2, ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_5]. A review compiling published field studies of agroforestry against its controls found average soil-loss reductions of 68% for silvopastoral systems, 66% for silvoarable agroforestry and 55% for linear tree plantings, with no significant difference among the system types, and average water-loss reductions of 73% for silvopastoral and 43% for silvoarable systems [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_3, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_1, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_2]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT compiler adds that, due to less wind and water erosion, the siltation of ponds and water pans is reduced [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers reported that tree roots prevented extensive soil erosion and soil fertility loss during the floods [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1]. During Hurricane Mitch in October 1998, Honduran farmers practising the Quesungual system suffered less landslide damage than those using traditional slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1]. In Costa Rica and Nicaragua, runoff equalled 28-48% of rainfall on pastures without trees against less than 10% in silvopastoral systems [ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1]. Runoff was higher on grass pasture than in tree-dominated fodder banks, so tree cover attenuates runoff and the soil erosion it causes [ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. Within single sub-practices, live fences of Gliricidia sepium are used to prevent erosion, shade trees attenuate runoff and erosion by close to a factor of two against full-sun plots, and in Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion erosion under silvopasture was 35.3 percent lower than on degraded pasture soils [ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_2, ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1]. In shaded perennial systems, a study on a Costa Rican coffee farm found shade trees reduced sheet erosion by a factor of 2 against full-sun plots [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1], and after Hurricane Stan in Chiapas, Mexico, coffee farms with more complex vegetation suffered less landslide damage [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_10]. Along field boundaries, on Saskatchewan prairie fields with old shelterbelts planted to reduce wind erosion, erosion midway between the belts has generally been much less than in unsheltered fields, judged from depth to carbonates and 137Cs, and the authors expect soil productivity there to be higher than in open fields [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report that soil erosion has been nearly stopped, and estimate nutrient loss through erosion at more than 10 times lower than under slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4]. A meta-analysis of seven African erosion-control studies (Kenya, Nigeria, Zimbabwe) found agroforestry outperformed controls by a response ratio of 5 for runoff and by 7.2 to 8 for soil loss depending on agro-ecological zone (humid vs semi-arid) [ev_runoff_reduction_kuyah19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_3]. A separate meta-analysis found infiltration rates 75% higher and runoff 57% lower under agroforestry than crop monoculture (an overall 50% reduction in soil erosion), and separated the erosion-rate response ratio by tree type: 0.29 for non-nitrogen-fixing trees against 0.41 for nitrogen-fixing trees (lower is less erosion), a difference the authors found was not statistically significant [ev_runoff_reduction_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_2, ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_3]. Agroforestry farmland is reported to be more resilient to heavy rainfall through a 20-50% decrease in runoff and an increase in soil-water infiltration [ev_runoff_reduction_dobhal24_2]. In Argentina, soil erosion and soil exhaustion under yerba mate grown as a monoculture were much lower when the crop was grown with trees in an agroforestry system [ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1]. In Costa Rica, shade trees are described as protecting soil from sheet erosion and conserving fertility through organic-matter inputs [ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11]. In Kenya, a farmer in Isiolo County explained that planting trees in a line prevents soil from being swept away by water [ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6]. IPCC assessments state in general terms that agroforestry limits soil erosion and helps stabilise soils against desertification, over an estimated extent of about 10 million km2 of land with more than 10% tree cover [ev_erosion_hazard_ipccar6ch5_5, ev_erosion_hazard_ipccsrccl6_2, ev_erosion_hazard_ipccsrccl6_5]. In Mexican coffee, the area affected by landslides significantly increased as vegetation complexity was reduced from forest to shaded monoculture [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_2]. The same Nigerian alley-cropping model also projects soil loss directly: over a 20-year horizon on a sloping field, 2 m-spaced Leucaena alley cropping gives the lowest predicted cumulative soil loss of the systems compared (2.5 t/ha), against 17.8 t/ha for the traditional short-cycle bush fallow it is compared with; 4 m spacing follows at 9.9 t/ha, still below the no-till (14 t/ha) and bush-fallow controls [ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_1, ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_2, ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_3]. On a steep hillslope in Laguna, the Philippines, a randomised trial of contour hedgerows (Desmanthus virgatus) on maize-mungbean alleys found annual soil loss fell step-wise with each added practice: from 124 t/ha/yr under the farmer's up-and-down-slope tillage, to 40 t/ha/yr once contour hedgerows and contour tillage were added, to 3 t/ha/yr once the hedgerow trimmings and crop residues were also spread as mulch, to 0.2 t/ha/yr once zero tillage was added on top of hedgerows and mulch; the hedgerow-plus-contour-tillage treatment alone also produced only about half as much annual runoff as the farmer's practice [ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_1, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_2, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_3, ev_runoff_reduction_paningbatan95_4]. In Jiangxi Province, China, a randomised trial intercropping peanut with Choerospondias axillaris trees on a sloping field found mean soil loss per rainfall event fell by 25.3% with younger trees and by 32.0% with older trees compared with mono-cropped peanut [ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_1, ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_2]. In Brazilian coffee, accumulated soil loss under shade was 26% of the loss measured in the unshaded area, and accumulated water loss was 44% of the unshaded area's, over the same rainy season [ev_erosion_hazard_decarvalho21_1, ev_runoff_reduction_decarvalho21_2]. In Niger, farmers and reviewers describe trees in the regenerated fields protecting against wind, reducing erosion and evaporation, and enriching the soil through litter decomposition and nutrients from livestock sheltering in their shade [ev_erosion_hazard_boton10_6]. A West African cocoa study notes, citing earlier work, that cocoa agroforestry with well-managed shade helps reduce erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_arizasal23_2]. A European model finds windbreaks would avoid about 13 Mt of soil loss by wind each year, 23% of total wind-erosion soil loss in the EU and UK [ev_erosion_hazard_englund21_9].
records.conditionality: The rating is moderate because the types of agroforestry differ: general findings, planted tree-crop alleys and silvopasture show strong reductions, linear boundary plantings a moderate one, and trees regenerated on farmland and shaded tree crops only small ones. The cross-practice syntheses agree on large reductions: the sub-Saharan and pantropical meta-analyses and the review of compiled field studies, whose averages hold across silvopastoral, silvoarable and linear plantings alike [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_3]. Single-practice field evidence is often weaker than those averages, so the size a project can expect depends on site and practice [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The compiled-review percentages are simple averages of study reductions, not weighted meta-analytic effects, and they mix temperate and tropical studies [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1]. The shade-tree effect represents little at catchment scale on the andisols studied [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3]. Site matters within a practice: erosion fell 35.3 percent in Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion but only 5.4 percent in the Cesar River Valley [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The sub-Saharan authors warn the very large effect sizes could reflect publication bias and expect more modest effects with more studies [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1]. Regreening Africa observed no large overall change in erosion prevalence and found no link between more trees on farm and lower erosion, the FMNR result is participants' reported erosion, and the Nicaraguan hurricane result bundles trees with terraces and contour planting [ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_3, ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_5, ev_erosion_hazard_wvfmnr19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_9]. The WOCAT finding is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not an erosion measurement, and the siltation rating enters as a component [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. The Lower Nyando erosion finding is farmer-reported, not measured [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1]. The landslide and runoff results are earlier studies cited in a working paper, a CATIE edited volume and a Spanish-language review; the runoff findings enter as components of erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1, ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1, ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. The Chiapas landslide results are crop-specific coffee evidence from a single hurricane, with the landslide-volume and landslide-size trends only marginal (P = 0.062) and no effect of nearby forest cover [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_5, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_4]. The Honduran erosion claim is a narrative from a promoter-written grey-literature article with no measured erosion rate, and the effect belongs to the whole bundle of trees, mulch cover, zero tillage and no burning [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt finding is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the low- and lower-middle-income countries this tool targets; it infers past erosion from soil markers and states no erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. In China, a field study of windbreak patches found windbreaks reduced average wind-erosion soil loss by 20% compared with open farmland [ev_erosion_hazard_chang21_1]. The Kenya/Nigeria/Zimbabwe meta-analysis breaks its result down by agro-ecological zone rather than giving one pooled number, and both erosion response ratios in it are large enough that, alongside the sub-Saharan meta-analysis already in this row, the same publication-bias caution applies [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_3]. Most of these newer findings are review or assessment statements rather than site measurements: the IPCC and farmland-resilience statements give no size or site, and the Argentine, Costa Rican and Kenyan farmer statements are a review citation, a Spanish-language case description and a single farmer's perception, not a measured erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_ipccar6ch5_5, ev_runoff_reduction_dobhal24_2, ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1, ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11, ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6]. The Chinese windbreak study and the Kenya/Nigeria/Zimbabwe meta-analysis add upper-middle-income and low- and lower-middle-income evidence respectively, broadly consistent with the row's existing transfer. The Nigerian erosion figures are modelled, not measured, running a simplified USLE-based erosion model calibrated to plot-level erosion rates from the same research station, and the model's own ranking shows erosion as time-dependent: initial erosion rates are lower under no-till than under the 4 m alley, with the alley only overtaking by the end of the 20-year horizon. The Philippines result is bundled: each successive treatment adds a co-practice (contour tillage, then mulch from the hedgerow trimmings and crop residues, then zero tillage) on top of the hedgerows, so the hedgerow-alone share of the reduction cannot be separated from the tillage and mulch changes that go with it, and even the hedgerow-plus-contour-tillage treatment is still called 'considerable' soil loss by the authors, not yet a tolerable rate. Both the Philippines and Nigeria results sit inside the low- and lower-middle-income countries this tool targets; the Chinese trial is upper-middle-income evidence. The same Chinese trial found a reversal on runoff: mean runoff per event was higher in both tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut, even though soil loss was lower — the authors attribute the higher runoff to surface seals and crusts forming on the untilled soil under and between the tree rows, while tillage of the peanut area itself raised infiltration there; this counts as measured harm for some adopters [ev_runoff_reduction_wei07_3]. Absolute losses were small in both the shaded and unshaded plots on this farm, so the shaded advantage sits on a very low base, and the comparison is a single-farm case study with no replication or significance test, upper-middle-income Brazilian evidence [ev_erosion_hazard_decarvalho21_1]. The cocoa erosion statement is second-hand and gives no size [ev_erosion_hazard_arizasal23_2]. The European wind-erosion figure is a model for high-income Europe [ev_erosion_hazard_englund21_9].

records.conditionality: The review-based average rests on a single review whose percentages are averages of compiled study reductions, not weighted meta-analytic effects, and which gives no country or income-group breakdown [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2]. records.mitigation_mechanism: The evidence points to a small reduction in flood impact, with no size given. Wooded riparian strips act on the water pathway rather than on the crop: they slow the flow of water from the land into receiving water bodies by increasing infiltration, reducing flow velocity and providing temporary storage [ev_flood_hazard_cole20_1], and mature woodland is the more effective form because of its structural complexity and the deadwood it delivers to the watercourse [ev_flood_hazard_cole20_2]. The only field finding runs from removal: in Marqués de Comillas, Chiapas, floods along with the seasonal drying of permanent streams and altered river dynamics were associated with the loss of riparian forest [ev_flood_hazard_meli19_4]. A European model of strips of willow, poplar or grass planted along watercourses rates the chance of reducing recurring floods as high or very high in about 1/7 to 1/5 of the landscapes where buffers are set up [ev_flood_hazard_englund21_8].
records.caveats: Nothing here is a measured reduction in flood damage to a farm. The Chiapas finding describes what losing riparian forest was associated with, in a case study, not what establishing a buffer delivers [ev_flood_hazard_meli19_4]. The European estimate is a model, and in most landscapes it does not rate the flood benefit as high [ev_flood_hazard_englund21_8]. The review that states the benefit confines it to moderate flooding and makes it depend on the extent, location, age and density of the woodland, with mature woodland more effective [ev_flood_hazard_cole20_2], which a new strip is not. No source reports a buffer holding up in a severe or extreme flood. The effect works on water moving into streams and rivers, so the farm giving up land need not be where the benefit lands. The sources are a UK review and a European model, both from rich, temperate countries, plus one upper-middle-income case from Mexico; there is no low-income evidence.

records.effect_mechanism: The rating is a small reduction in erosion risk. Most of the large percentages below measure runoff and soil caught in the strip at the stream edge; the one estimate of soil loss avoided on the cropland itself is small. The buffer intercepts overland flow before it reaches the channel: dense switchgrass stops concentrated flow from the field and allows infiltration rates well above the field rate [ev_runoff_reduction_schultz95_1], which cut runoff by 58.3% behind a 7 m switchgrass buffer and 81.5% behind the wider switchgrass-woody buffer over 19 natural events [ev_runoff_reduction_lee03_5, ev_runoff_reduction_lee03_6], and by more than 77% in Kansas grass-shrub plots [ev_runoff_reduction_mank07_2]. What the water no longer carries is trapped: 70% of incoming sediment behind the grass buffer and more than 92% behind the grass-woody buffer under simulated rainfall [ev_sediment_retention_lee00_1, ev_sediment_retention_lee00_2], 95% and 97% over natural events [ev_sediment_retention_lee03_1, ev_sediment_retention_lee03_3] with trapping never falling below 71% in any storm [ev_sediment_retention_lee03_7], 99.7% of suspended-solids mass in pumped-runoff plots [ev_sediment_retention_mank07_1], 97% behind an 8 m grass strip and 91% within the first 4 m [ev_sediment_retention_blanco04_1, ev_sediment_retention_blanco04_4, ev_sediment_retention_blanco04_2, ev_sediment_retention_blanco04_3], and 92% for woody, 72% for grass and 50% for shrub strips in the Guishui catchment against a bare control that trapped 22% [ev_sediment_retention_kumw24_1, ev_sediment_retention_kumw24_2, ev_sediment_retention_kumw24_3]. Trapping efficiency rises sharply over the first 10 m and then tails off [ev_sediment_retention_cole20_1], and narrow strips are already effective [ev_sediment_retention_osbo93_15, ev_sediment_retention_lee04_1, ev_sediment_retention_lee04_3, ev_sediment_retention_schultz95_1, ev_sediment_retention_zhao13_1, ev_sediment_retention_clau00_1]; in Brazilian third-order watersheds, suspended and organic solids fall as riparian forest cover rises [ev_sediment_retention_mello18_1, ev_sediment_retention_mello18_2], and a national model adds 3.9% to sediment retention [ev_sediment_retention_lang22_1]. A US riparian zone that had been cleared and cropped for a long time and was then restored to grass cut sediment concentration in overland flow by 92% [ev_sediment_retention_dosskey10_5], and McKergow et al. (2003) found that vegetation restoration of denuded, livestock-trampled riparian zones reduced catchment sediment export from over 100 to less than 10 kilograms per hectare per year within one year, mainly by reducing bank erosion and stabilising the stream channel [ev_sediment_retention_dosskey10_6]. The second pathway is the bank itself: planting trees stabilises river banks, reducing erosion and sediment loss [ev_streambank_erosion_cole20_1, ev_streambank_erosion_osbo93_17], willow posts held further collapse to an additional 0.3 m of bank through the 1993 floods and streambank integrity was maintained on the planted reach [ev_streambank_erosion_schultz95_1, ev_streambank_erosion_schultz95_2], farmers on the Ayuquila identify tree roots as what avoids riverbank erosion during floods [ev_streambank_erosion_meli19_5], and replacing riparian forest with other land cover brings bank erosion [ev_streambank_erosion_mello18_11]. A European model of strips of willow, poplar or grass planted along watercourses finds they avoid 6.3% of the soil lost to water erosion on cropland in the landscapes where they are set up (1.2% across the EU and UK), and separately catch 19% of all soil lost by water erosion on European cropland [ev_erosion_hazard_englund21_5, ev_sediment_retention_englund21_6].
records.conditionality: What the buffer traps depends on what the soil is made of: the same plots retained 93% of sand and silt but only 52% of clay [ev_sediment_retention_lee00_3], and a 4 m grass buffer on a 2% slope was almost 100% effective on sandy loams but only 35% effective on silty clay loams [ev_sediment_retention_cole20_2]. Width buys less than it appears to: retention rises sharply over the first 10 m and then tails off [ev_sediment_retention_cole20_1], widening from 50 m to 100 m added only 4.6% and 4.0% in the two models tested [ev_sediment_retention_sira20_2], and 30 m buffers were unable to prevent increases in stream sedimentation after partial clearcutting [ev_sediment_retention_lee04_2]. Most of the large percentages come from plot-scale experiments under simulated rainfall or pumped runoff rather than field-scale monitoring [ev_sediment_retention_mank07_1, ev_sediment_retention_lee00_1, ev_sediment_retention_blanco04_1], and the mass reductions are achieved partly because water infiltrates and is lost, which is not the same as a cleaner stream [ev_runoff_reduction_mank07_2]. Two of the strongest-looking numbers are modelled rather than measured — the 30.5 and 36.2% retention gains from widening Prince Edward Island buffers [ev_sediment_retention_sira20_1] and the Costa Rican 3.9% [ev_sediment_retention_lang22_1] — and the Brazilian values are correlations across a handful of watersheds, not experiments [ev_sediment_retention_mello18_1, ev_sediment_retention_mello18_2]. Two of the bank findings are farmer perception and cited background rather than measurement [ev_streambank_erosion_meli19_5, ev_streambank_erosion_mello18_11]. The two Dosskey-reviewed findings above are themselves citations of other studies, not new measurement by Dosskey et al. [ev_sediment_retention_dosskey10_5, ev_sediment_retention_dosskey10_6]. The measured core is narrow in origin: repeated studies on one Iowa stream, Bear Creek, supply a large share of the runoff and sediment figures [ev_runoff_reduction_lee03_5, ev_sediment_retention_lee00_1, ev_sediment_retention_lee03_1, ev_runoff_reduction_schultz95_1], alongside Kansas, Missouri and Connecticut plots; apart from China and Brazil the whole pool is temperate high-income, and no measurement comes from a low-income farming system. The European figures are model results from rich countries [ev_erosion_hazard_englund21_5, ev_sediment_retention_englund21_6].

records.mitigation_mechanism: Restored and protected forest burns less where people actively guard it. In India villagers protect the forest intervention area from anthropogenic and wild fires, and the compiler reports that the forest has rehabilitated more quickly and has a lower risk of burning due to improved green vegetation cover and less flammable pine needle accumulation [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_5243_2019_fire_risk]. In Tanzania the compiler for an enclosure rates bush-fire hazard as reduced due to the enclosure, fire breaks and the use of bylaws [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_1607_2014_fire_risk]. A World Bank evaluation lists reduced incidence of fires among the environmental outcomes that participatory forest management projects reported where those outcomes were monitored [ev_fire_hazard_ieg13_1].
records.caveats: Every unit that gives a reason names active fire management (village guarding, fire breaks, bylaws), so the reduction should not be assumed where closure or planting comes without fire protection in the design [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_5243_2019_fire_risk, ev_fire_hazard_wocat_1607_2014_fire_risk]. The field units are practitioner ratings, not measurements, and the World Bank evaluation is a portfolio-level narrative without magnitudes that covers only projects that monitored the outcome [ev_fire_hazard_ieg13_1]. No unit covers severe or extreme fire. The effect is off-site for farmers: it applies to the restored forest and the landscape around it, not to their plots.

records.mitigation_mechanism: In this evidence restored forest cover lowers flood peaks moderately, and mainly at local scale and for smaller storms. Catchment models show it: in Slovakia's Hornad watershed a reforestation scenario cut a simulated flood peak from 84.8 to 74.9 m3/s and, for a 50% increase of forest, reduced peaks by about 24% on average in rain-duration tests, more for short storms than long ones [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_1, ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_3], and an afforestation simulation for Luxembourg's Alzette basin decreased the peak by 8% [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_5]. A systematic review of forest cover and catchment flooding finds peak flow changes by roughly half the change in forest cover, so a 20% increase in forest cover tends to reduce peak flow by 10% across small, medium and large catchments, with only minor differences in mean reductions across event intensities up to the 1% AEP event; the review attributes this to forests detaining floodwater through infiltration, canopy interception and evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_1, ev_flood_hazard_herath25_5]. Another systematic review found that flooding or peak flows decreased with forest cover expansion in 82% of the studies reporting them [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1]. A UNESCO review of moist tropical forest hydrology states that the beneficial effects of reforesting, terracing and contouring degraded lands on stormflow and peakflow are evident at small-basin scale, as is the regenerative capacity of most ecosystems when left alone [ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_6, ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_7]. In a clear-cut Oregon basin, peak discharges recovered gradually as the basin revegetated, which the authors attribute to changes in evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. An FAO synthesis expects flash flooding to be reduced locally for frequent short, low-intensity storm events where soils are deep [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_7], and a global review states that afforestation in energy-limited environments will help to reduce flood risks [ev_flood_hazard_zhang17_1]. An Ethiopian WOCAT compiler for a regeneration-based technology rates downstream flooding as strongly reduced, noting that runoff from the watershed is highly reduced [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1072_2011_downstream_flooding]. A global study of natural climate solutions also lists flood control among reforestation's well-demonstrated co-benefits, citing an earlier assessment, with no size given [ev_flood_hazard_griscom17_3].
records.caveats: What separates the benefit from the nulls is scale and storm size. The gains are local, modelled or small-storm results; the nulls are about large basins and floods on the plains. The FAO synthesis finds no evidence that reforesting watersheds reduces or prevents floods except at the very local scale of a few hundred hectares [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_5, ev_flood_hazard_ham08_6]. A Himalayan analysis concludes that reforestation will not likely have significant beneficial impact on local flooding, and certainly not on the hydrological character of the Ganges and Brahmaputra mainstreams [ev_flood_hazard_ives87_1], and a conference overview warns that reforestation in the mountains conceived as a palliative for the problems of the plains is likely to reap only disappointment [ev_flood_hazard_ivesmt87_1], and both come from the same lead author, so they count as a single line of argument. An FAO–CIFOR review concludes that massive programmes of forestation proclaimed as the answer to preventing floods simply will not do the job, although reforestation may have many other benefits [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_3], and a published comment argues that reforestation does not necessarily reduce flooding, for example if soil properties do not recover, river bed morphology does not change, and settlements, roads and drains remain unaltered [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_5]. A review of coastal tree belts adds a coastal null: the science on short-period wave damping should not be taken to show that vegetation can reduce the effects of storm surges [ev_flood_hazard_feagin10_1]; this is an expert argument about coastal plantings, not a measurement. These are expert positions and reviews rather than new measurements. The co-benefit listing is second-hand and states no size, place or scale [ev_flood_hazard_griscom17_3]. The UNESCO review's statement is local only, its supporting table cannot be read so no size is available, and the planting half of the sentence pools reforesting with terracing and contouring, so it cannot be credited to trees alone [ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_6, ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_7]. The flood-cover review adds that afforestation yields only gradual reductions, smaller than the rises in peak flow that follow deforestation and shaped by forest maturity, with peak flow in small catchments falling by up to 14% on limited data [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_2, ev_flood_hazard_herath25_4]; its pooled peak-flow points come from modelled scenarios in mostly temperate catchments, so it is a synthesis of other studies' models rather than new measurement. The modelled benefit itself shrinks as rain continues, from 29% for the shortest rain duration to 17% for the longest [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_3], and all catchment models are scenarios of large forest-cover gains in temperate high-income basins; the largest figure, a 42.3% peak reduction from converting all arable land to forest, is a secondary citation with no basin named [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_4]. The Oregon recovery comes from a clear-cut harvest study, measured against the freshly cut state rather than against unrestored land, and the paper does not say whether the regrowth was planted or natural [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. The low- and lower-middle-income evidence is a compiler rating and expert positions, not measured flows or flood damage. The forest-water review pools restoration with forestry and afforestation and reports vote counts rather than magnitudes [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1]. No unit measures a benefit at severe or extreme flood; the only reading at the 1% AEP event is that review's pooled modelled points [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_5]. Studies of what existing forest does, such as harvest experiments and the Himalayan essays on forest loss, sit in the protection family row and do not set this class. For farmers the effect is off-site: any reduction arrives downstream of the restored land, not on their plots.

records.effect_mechanism: Tree cover reduces erosion by protecting the soil surface, slowing runoff and holding slopes, and the sub-practice rows agree on that direction. A UNESCO review of moist tropical forest hydrology locates the surface protection in the litter and herb layer: erosion is minimal where the soil surface is protected by a well-developed litter and herb layer, rises only slightly when the understorey is removed, and rises dramatically when the litter layer is destroyed or removed [ev_erosion_hazard_bruij90_10]. The same review states that tree planting, like soil conservation measures, may well reduce the sediment from surface erosion and shallow land slips entering the drainage system [ev_sediment_retention_bruij90_13]. In the passive regeneration evidence, an Ethiopian meta-analysis finds areas closed for grazing and agriculture had runoff coefficients of 4% against 19% on control sites [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_1], the Tanzanian enclosure compiler rates surface runoff as decreased as a result of vegetation cover and downstream siltation as decreased through improved vegetation cover and controlled erosion [ev_runoff_reduction_wocat_1607_2014_surface_runoff, ev_sediment_retention_wocat_1607_2014_downstream_siltation], and the higher probability of landslides after timber removal diminishes substantially 15–25 yr after harvesting as replacement trees mature [ev_erosion_hazard_sidle06_2]. The planting evidence carries the measured magnitudes: in Pakistan a watershed restoration reduced storm runoff and sediment yields by 55 and 78% [ev_runoff_reduction_hanif90_1, ev_erosion_hazard_hanif90_1], Chir pine planting with elimination of grazing at Balakot reduced surface runoff by 57% and sediment production by 69% against adjacent grazed land [ev_runoff_reduction_hanif90_2], tree planting on degraded Ethiopian catchments cut annual runoff from 242 to 148 mm/year [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_2], and vegetation restoration in China could reduce soil erosion by at least 80% once cover exceeds 60% [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_1]. A Slovak catchment model shows reforestation decreasing surface runoff [ev_runoff_reduction_bahremand06_1]. A meta-analysis of vegetation restoration in erosion zones finds that both forestland and grassland restoration of cropland or bare land were effective methods for controlling erosion, cutting sediment and runoff, with canopies, root systems and the organic surface layer not differing in their impact [ev_erosion_hazard_yang23_1, ev_runoff_reduction_yang23_2]. In Tigray, Ethiopia, upstream treatment with deep trenches, percolation pits and afforestation reduced siltation of May Demu dam by up to 60%, a figure the chapter takes from Woldearegay's earlier 2011 report, and in the Abreha Weatsbeha watershed the authors observed significant improvements in reducing soil erosion after afforestation, area closures and water-harvesting works [ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_3, ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_1]. FAO syntheses call forest restoration one of the best ways of reducing sedimentation in degraded cleared land, list reducing soil loss among the very good reasons for rehabilitating watersheds, and cite Taiwan, where a rehabilitation programme reduced reservoir sedimentation by 55 percent of the base rate [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_1, ev_erosion_hazard_ham08_1, ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. An FAO review of forests and landslides in Asia asserts that tree planting on susceptible slopes can reduce risk [ev_erosion_hazard_forbes11_1], and land abandonment with an increase in forest and grassland led to less soil erosion in one cited case [ev_erosion_hazard_iufro18_5]. At community-managed sites the India compiler credits trees and other vegetation with mitigating displacement of soil from upstream areas to the lowlands and with slowing sediment and runoff [ev_erosion_hazard_wocat_5243_2019_soil_loss, ev_sediment_retention_wocat_5243_2019_downstream_siltation], and a World Bank evaluation lists reduced soil erosion among the outcomes participatory forest management projects reported where they were monitored [ev_erosion_hazard_ieg13_1].
records.conditionality: The benefit is largely off-site for farmers: much of it is reduced runoff and sediment reaching downstream land and channels rather than better soil on their own plots [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_5243_2019_downstream_siltation]. Scale and time limit the downstream effect. The UNESCO review warns that, because of storage effects, it may take several decades for basins larger than several hundred square kilometres before stream sediment loads downstream become noticeably smaller [ev_sediment_retention_bruij90_14]. Nulls and dissent stay named. In China the soil conservation measures, including vegetation and engineering, contributed 12.1–13.9% sediment reduction in the Three-Gorge Reservoir Area, so the vegetation share should be less than 10% in most instances [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_2]; decreased Pearl River sediment loads had little to do with soil conservation measures [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_3]; and on the Loess Plateau an inversely decreasing trend of erosion reduction with vegetation cover was attributed to the immaturity of the planted species [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_4]. A Himalayan position paper judges that reforestation will not likely have significant beneficial impact on soil loss [ev_erosion_hazard_ives87_1], young second-growth timber falls far short of providing the root support of its older predecessors [ev_erosion_hazard_bishop64_5], abandoned land in previously terraced landscapes can be particularly prone to gully erosion and landslides [ev_erosion_hazard_iufro18_4], and the REDD+ pilot in Nepal had an insignificant effect on signs of soil erosion in community forests (SMD = −0.15, 95% CI [−0.31, 0.02]) [ev_erosion_hazard_snilstveit19_1]. The largest measured reductions are bundles: the Pakistan results combine planting with grazing control and, in the watershed study, erosion control structures, and the Taiwan programme combines reforestation with soil conservation on cultivated land, fire control and check dams, so none can be credited to tree cover alone [ev_erosion_hazard_hanif90_1, ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. The Tigray results are bundles of afforestation and area closures with trenches, percolation pits and check-dams, from showcase sites, and the dam figure is an upper bound carried from an earlier report [ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_3, ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_1]. The UNESCO sediment statement also offers tree planting as one option among soil conservation measures, not as a measured tree effect [ev_sediment_retention_bruij90_13]. The erosion-zone meta-analysis reports its forest-only effect sizes only in a figure, so it sets the direction but not a size [ev_erosion_hazard_yang23_1]. The runoff results measure a component of erosion risk rather than soil loss [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_1]. Studies of what existing forest does, including logging and harvest landslide studies, sit in the protection family row and do not count here, and plantation results are kept in their own family row, out of this roll-up.
